items.title: This 1968 Shelby Mustang GT350 Is Seriously Rare. That Didn’t Stop the Owner From Supercharging It
items.summary:
When it comes to investment-grade collector vehicles, there are few safer bets than a 1960s muscle car. And if you want to hedge your bet, a Shelby Mustang is a good way to go. The original Mustang is legendary, the Ford partnership with Shelby American even more so. But despite the potential value tied up in this 1968 Shelby Mustang GT350 convertible’s sheetmetal and woodgrain dash and door-panel appliqués, the selling owner wasn’t afraid of modifying it.

Currently up for auction on Bring a Trailer , this car is one of just 404 GT350 convertibles built for the 1968 model year. It was restored in 2020, now shows 32,000 miles, and has the factory-correct 302-cubic-inch V8. But that engine is now topped with a Paxton supercharger installed after the seller bought the car. The seller also swapped the original three-speed automatic transmission for a five-speed manual. The supercharger is at least a period-correct modification, but no such excuse can be made for the modern Flowmaster exhaust system. All the removed original parts are included with the sale.

B 

Credit: Bring a Trailer 

The Mustang may have had the biggest launch of any new car in history, but Ford wanted to keep that momentum going. And under its Total Performance program, the automaker used racing as its primary marketing tool. So it asked Shelby to turn the Mustang into a race car, and the GT350 was born. The original 1965 model was intended for SCCA racing, but Ford and Shelby quickly realized that customers wanted a more refined road car with sporty styling more than a track toy.

The 1968 Shelby…
items.t: This 1968 Shelby Mustang GT350 Is Seriously Rare. That Didn’t Stop the Owner From Supercharging It

items.title: Can’t Pass Emissions With Your Pre-OBD-II Car? Have Claude Tune It for You
items.summary:
Artificial intelligence has been crowned as the next big thing by whoever makes those decisions. It’s now being implemented across the auto industry , and despite all the hype, we mostly seem to be finding out what it can’t do , and that it requires a lot of memory to achieve even that disappointing level of performance. But one YouTuber claims to have found a very good use for Claude.

Muhammad Zulali has a 1994 Jeep Cherokee that failed California emissions tests. Because it’s a 1994 model, this XJ Cherokee doesn’t have an OBD-II port, so Zulali couldn’t plug in a generic scanning tool to look for trouble codes. There was a Chrysler-specific scanning tool compatible with vehicles from this model year, but it’s hard to find these days and doesn’t provide much information anyway, Zulali explains in the video.

Muhammad Zulali via YouTube 

Looking for an alternative way to read data from the car’s onboard computer, Zulali says he asked Claude, which identified the computer’s communication protocol and suggested using an Arduino Nano to translate it. Arduino makes open-source microcontrollers that are prized in the maker community for their flexibility, and they can come in handy when doing engine swaps involving different manufacturers’ computer controls as well. This one cost just $3.

That allowed Claude to take readings from the Cherokee’s computer, but the first ones created more questions than answers. Thinking that low fuel pressure might be the issue, Zulali began testing that—and found out that Claude could do more than just passively read data. He said the model…

items.title: A Ford Maverick Will Fit a Gnarly Twin-Turbo V8—With a Whole Lot of Work
items.summary:
When the Ford Maverick arrived in 2021, it revived the compact truck segment that has long been a favorite of tuners and customizers. So it’s not surprising that we’ve seen quite a few modified Mavericks in the short time this pickup has been on sale. Yet there’s one obvious thing no one attempted until now: a V8 swap.

Tucci Hot Rods finally rectified that at the 2026 SEMA show, where it unveiled a 2022 Maverick with a twin-turbo Coyote V8. If you’re not familiar with this Upstate New York shop, it was one of the first that Ford partnered with on Maverick SEMA builds back in 2021. Tucci’s first go was a 2.0-liter EcoBoost truck with 3D-printed parts that gave it a serious street-truck vibe. Ford cited that build as one of the inspirations for the Maverick Lobo , in fact. Now, Tucci has Coyote-swapped that truck.

Credit: Tucci Hot Rods via Facebook 

“When we originally built the truck in 2021 for Ford, it was a pre-production vehicle. The build went over really well, and afterward, we joked that we should Coyote-swap it,” Tucci Hot Rods owner Dave Tucci told Ford Muscle . “Eventually, that joke turned into a real plan.”

As detailed in a post by Engine Swap Depot , Tucci paired Ford’s ubiquitous 5.0-liter V8 with a pair of Hellion 62 millimeter turbos. The engine was also treated to a new intake manifold, oil pan, and fuel rails, while the exhaust was routed through the Maverick’s front fender vents using custom 3D-printed pieces. The setup is good for up to 1,200 horsepower.

Credit: Tucci Hot Rods via Facebook 

The engine is connected to a ZF 8HP70 eight-speed…
items.t: A Ford Maverick Will Fit a Gnarly Twin-Turbo V8—With a Whole Lot of Work

items.title: Welding This 109-Year-Old Engine Back Together Has Turned Into a Community Effort
items.summary:
There’s no instruction manual for repairing century-old hardware, let alone modifying it for different purposes. And the older something gets, the less likely it is that someone who worked on it in-period will be around to offer advice. While the Internet has become a disappointment in so many ways, it can still live up to its promise as a way to connect with people and get information that would otherwise be unavailable.

Dominic Chinea, a former set designer and cast member of the BBC show The Repair Shop, is working on something ambitious. As documented on his YouTube channel , Chinea is building an aero-engined race car in the style of the specials that were popular on the Edwardian-era British racing scene. He’s combining a 1912 Rochet-Schneider chassis with a 1917 Liberty V12 airplane engine into something eligible for vintage racing —specifically, the Goodwood Members’ Meeting. That means using only period-correct components and techniques, which presents a major issue.

Credit: Dominic Chinea via T 

Just after World War I, airplane engines were coveted by racers for their power density. They produced much more power for their weight than automotive engines of the time. They were also pretty easy to get ahold of. The Liberty engine was mass produced for the war effort, so there were plenty of leftovers; however, the V12 was too long for the chassis, so Chinea decided to cut it in half and weld it back together as a V8. The Liberty engine block is really two large pieces—an upper half containing the cylinders and a lower half containing the crankcase and sump—but…
items.t: Welding This 109-Year-Old Engine Back Together Has Turned Into a Community Effort

items.title: Look at This Strange Supercar With a Sportbike Seating Position
items.summary:
Automotive startups are as common as billet at SEMA, but Dutch startup Sanrivatti has a unique gimmick. It’s developing a supercar with a motorcycle-style seating position. What Sanrivatti has coined as the “Apex Position” calls for the driver to straddle a central tunnel while still being fully ensconced in a cockpit. Sanrivatti first teased this concept earlier this year, but now we know a little more about this strange supercar.

Dubbed the Sanrivatti One, it has the outrageous specs that are obligatory in the supercar world. According to the company’s website , it’s targeting 800 horsepower at 9,000 rpm, as well as 516 pound-feet of torque, from a powertrain of unspecified design. The target dry weight is 2,425 pounds, and the targeted top speed is 205 mph.

Credit: Sanrivatti 

Sanrivatti has also released renderings of the car, which don’t reveal any surprises. The body is a collection of airflow channels necessary to keep the One stable at that ambitious top speed. There’s a big rear spoiler hung off the back and an endurance prototype-style stabilizer fin that should also help with that. The cockpit is very narrow, which makes sense given the unusual seating position. It may also provide some aerodynamic benefits by reducing the car’s frontal area.

It’s still unclear when we’ll see the Sanrivatti One in production-ready form, but the startup has been testing its straddle seat with digital simulations and a modified 986 Porsche Boxster. Sanrivatti claims that simulations show that drivers get a much better view, seeing up to 3.2 times more of their surroundings at…
items.t: Look at This Strange Supercar With a Sportbike Seating Position

items.title: You Can Spend Hours Designing Roll Cages With This Free Online Tool
items.summary:
If you’re going racing, you need a roll cage . But there often isn’t an off-the-rack option that meets the requirements of the series you plan to race in—one that provides adequate protection and actually fits in your car. Get the design wrong, and you’ll waste a lot of time and material. Now there’s a free online tool to help ensure that doesn’t happen.

Frog Racing , a Massachusetts-based nonprofit that promotes motorsports, has a number of helpful guides and tools for aspiring racers. One of them is its roll cage assessment tool , which can build a virtual roll cage based on parameters you specify like the tubing, welds, and layout, and then compare it against different sanctioning bodies’ rulebooks to find out if it’s legal as well as assign a safety score.

Credit: Frog Racing 

The tool is pre-loaded with sample cages, including real-world examples, commercially available kits, and generic examples like a half cage, NHRA-compliant drag racing cage, and an FIA Article 253 Appendix J cage (the tool’s safety score is also based on Article 253). There’s even a “worst cage” that shows you everything not to do. You can also start from scratch and design a cage with the tool, or import a file with an existing design.

The tool includes a questionnaire that starts with basics like a car’s year, make, and model, and whether it’s left- or righthand drive, and continues with other pertinent information like the type of tubing and welds being used, location of bars and gussets, and any dimensional constraints of a car’s cockpit. You can also upload photos and have the tool…
items.t: You Can Spend Hours Designing Roll Cages With This Free Online Tool

items.title: Finally, a NASCAR Ford Mustang That Looks Like the Real Thing
items.summary:
NASCAR stock cars used to actually be stock , but that hasn’t been the case for a while. Automaker still use road-car branding for their NASCAR entries, though, and the current-generation Cup Series cars are a much better canvas for road-car styling than the previous generation. One of the best efforts so far is the updated Mustang that Ford will race in 2027, starting with Daytona Speedweeks.

When Ford announced the Mustang Dark Horse SC in January, it confirmed that the nameplate would replace the standard Dark Horse in the Cup Series. Now we know what the updated car looks like, and it’s a solid effort to superimpose the design of the seventh-generation Mustang road car onto the seventh-generation Cup Series car. The front end makes it easier to suspend disbelief about the headlights and grille being stickers, and the rear fenders have prominent haunches like the road car’s.

Ford 

Ford 

It’s impressive that the Dark Horse SC Cup car and road car look even a little alike considering how different the engineering requirements are for each. As Ford noted in a press release, the front end of the road car was designed to prioritize cooling, hence the many large openings that exist only as stickers on the Cup car. The emphasis there was on downforce, which is obviously more important on a car that spends most of its time running at high speeds. And that’s not even accounting for the long list of federal regulations and the thick NASCAR rule book that the road car and race car must comply with, respectively.

The current Cup car design was introduced in 2022, bringing…
items.t: Finally, a NASCAR Ford Mustang That Looks Like the Real Thing
